new_candidates.title: A Bridge into Business
new_candidates.text: A bridge, a river, and shops almost at your feet. Researchers describe this part of Mudu as a busy commercial district. With shopfronts opening toward the waterfront, crossing the river could bring you straight into the market. A handy place to combine two errands!
new_candidates.observed: High arched bridge beside a continuous waterfront shop row; steps, pedestrians, boats and open shopfronts are visible.
new_candidates.evidence: Study: Mudu paragraph beginning 作者以木渎镇. The same market sequence contains the distinctive pavilion behind the shops and the wedding boats farther left. The commercial district is supported; the precise named bridge is not established independently.
new_candidates.guard: Removed the specific oblique-bridge identity. No shop trades, ownership, or actual errands assigned to individuals.
new_candidates.zoom: 750 x 460 scene; bridge remains readable at native scale. Bottom margin only 10 px: retain full source height in context and do not force vertical centering.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: A Temple Behind the Shops?
new_candidates.text: Shopfronts in front, a temple tucked behind! Researchers identify this enclosed compound by its two-storey, many-sided pavilion and aligned halls. The market street wasn't the whole town: religious buildings shared the same crowded waterfront neighborhood. Look past the first row of roofs for a different story.
new_candidates.observed: Two visible levels of the red polygonal pavilion, enclosed court, and receding aligned halls behind shops.
new_candidates.evidence: S1 Mudu paragraph: temple behind shop row, a two-level polygonal pavilion, an enclosed court, and halls in sequence. All spatial features are matched in the context. Six sides, a statue and two monks are described in the study but cannot be independently resolved here.
new_candidates.guard: Temple identity is attributed, not read from an inscription. No temple name, deity, ritual or exact side count.
new_candidates.zoom: Native evidence detail 620×310; focus scene 620×250 retains pavilion and halls. Keep surrounding roofs visible for the behind-the-shops relationship.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: A Granary with a Backup Plan
new_candidates.text: Those long roofs had a practical purpose. Researchers identify this waterside compound as a shecang, or community granary. Such granaries held grain to help communities withstand shortages. The rows of storehouses make a useful counterpoint to all those shops: prosperity needed a backup plan, too.
new_candidates.observed: Rectangular stone platform surrounded by water, four repeated roof rows, enclosed yard and long rear buildings.
new_candidates.evidence: S1 granary paragraph: a rectangular compound on a stone base, four repeated storehouse rows, beside water. Raw context shows the base and water; detail resolves the four foreground roof rows. S3 supplies the general relief function only.
new_candidates.guard: Wall signs are not transcribed. Grain storage function is a scholarly identification; no particular crop, stock amount, lending operation or worker identity is visible.
new_candidates.zoom: 1000 x 420 scene. Garden #05 is below and left; marker chosen on upper storehouse block. Green reproduction seam remains intact. Context touches top boundary; avoid cropping warehouse roofs.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: Farming at the Water's Edge
new_candidates.text: Not quite an empty lake! Low banks divide this waterside landscape into plots. Researchers describe fields and fishponds around Stone Lake, where people adapted the watery surroundings for food production. The shoreline was a working landscape as well as a scenic one. Look between the banks.
new_candidates.observed: Repeated low embankments enclose small plots and water areas; cultivated-looking strips differ from open lake beyond.
new_candidates.evidence: S1 Stone Lake paragraph: cultivation within the waterscape and enclosed fishponds. Detail shows multiple physically divided enclosures and banks, rather than empty lake. Individual enclosure use cannot be separated confidently into field versus fishpond.
new_candidates.guard: Say fields and fishponds in the Stone Lake landscape; never label a specific selected cell as a fishpond, fish trap, crop species or engineering technique.
new_candidates.zoom: Native 550×280 detail shows bank outlines; keep 1700×670 context to explain the lake setting. Low relief remains subtle without contrast enhancement.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: A Pagoda Above the Rooftops
new_candidates.text: City walls and a temple tower share this skyline. Researchers identify them as Panmen and Ruiguang Pagoda. One marked the fortified city edge; the other belonged to a Buddhist temple. Follow the wall, then look up: Suzhou's religious landscape rises just behind its defenses.
new_candidates.observed: Narrow tiered tower behind crenellated city wall, with gate precinct visible to its left in wider context.
new_candidates.evidence: S1 first city segment pairs Panmen and Ruiguang Pagoda in the distance, above the near Huai-Xu Bridge scene. Native context shows the gate precinct to the left, wall and tower behind; the sequence precedes Xumen. S6 independently supports the tower’s Buddhist temple association, not the pixel placement.
new_candidates.guard: Identification rests on the landmark pairing and scroll sequence, not a readable label. No age, tier count, relics, tilt, or historical construction claim.
new_candidates.zoom: Native tower/wall detail 350×285, no enlargement. The actual tower is narrow. Main 1080×325 scene keeps gate and tower together; on a 390px screen the detail area is about109×89px at the estimated scene scale. Inspect shape, not tiny architectural parts.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: Where the Boats Met the Street
new_candidates.text: A river journey still needed a way ashore. Researchers identify this busy landing beside the city wall as Xumen wharf. Stone embankments and steps connect the water to the crowded shore, with boats gathered alongside. Here, Suzhou's water traffic met its streets. Quite a change of pace!
new_candidates.observed: Stone quay, descending stairs, densely gathered figures and moored boats under the wall; gate context visible to left.
new_candidates.evidence: Study second city paragraph identifies Xumen wharf through the open landing outside the gate, raised stone embankment and steps, with warehouses and boat businesses nearby.
new_candidates.guard: No ceremony/event identification, cargo, occupational identities, loading action or specific warehouse use inferred for an individual roof.
new_candidates.zoom: 770 x 420 focus; crowded detail is readable as a group. Context is 1500 px wide and should be shown smaller; steps at marker remain principal visual target.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: A Bridge in Two Colors
new_candidates.text: Stone here, red-painted wood there. Researchers identify this as Wannian Bridge outside Xumen, with alternating stone and red wooden railings. Look along the parapet to spot the changing pattern. In this busy waterfront scene, even a river crossing came dressed for the occasion.
new_candidates.observed: Large stepped bridge across the moat, pale parapet sections alternating with red lattice sections, roofed pavilions and archway on approaches.
new_candidates.evidence: S1 second city segment and S2 p50 describe Wannian Bridge, approach pavilions/archways and alternating stone/red wooden parapets. The native detail resolves that alternating pattern; context fixes the bridge outside the wall beside Xumen. S5 independently confirms Wannian crosses the moat outside Xumen.
new_candidates.guard: Material identification attributed to research: pixels alone establish colors/pattern, not wood species. No need to read bridge name, count all openings in this crop, invent a festival, or reuse modern bridge images.
new_candidates.zoom: Wide 1160×440 scene reaches original lower edge; native detail 500×245 resolves railings. Context shows relation to quay and wall. Keep upper deck/pavilion visible; lower bridge continues beyond scan edge.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: Flags Mean Official Business
new_candidates.text: Those flags signal a different kind of business. Researchers identify this compound as the provincial administration office. Qing provincial commissioners had to report money and grain accounts as part of their duties. Prosperity came with paperwork, too. The fenced entrance gives official business a space of its own.
new_candidates.observed: Paired poles and yellow flags above fenced forecourt, screen, gatehouse and sequence of halls behind.
new_candidates.evidence: S1 third city segment: paired yellow flags, fenced forecourt, screen opposite the entry hall, and repeated axial halls. These features coincide in the native context/detail. S4 supplies general reporting duties of Qing provincial commissioners; its Jiangxi edict is not an account of this Suzhou scene.
new_candidates.guard: No independent reading of tiny flag lettering. No unseen document, named official, ceremony, or work taking place is asserted. Distinguish this compound from the examination precinct nearer Xumen.
new_candidates.zoom: 500 x 420 scene; paired poles and fence remain visible at native scale. Wider context necessary for axial compound; avoid selecting crowded street to right as focus.
new_candidates.confidence_explanation: High visual = real, identifiable structure/feature. Identification confidence assesses its historical label. Medium labels retain explicit research attribution; general history is separately sourced.

new_candidates.title: Room for Boats, Too
new_candidates.text: Up and over for people; room underneath for boats. This arched bridge belongs to the Shantang stretch of the scroll. Research on the painting explains how raised bridge openings accommodated water traffic while linking the banks. Two routes crossing in one small space. Nicely done, bridge builders.
new_candidates.observed: Large single arched bridge crossing the canal with people on steps and a boat adjacent to the opening.
new_candidates.evidence: Bridge study p50 on raised arches and navigation, p51 on Shantang bridges; museum route places Shantang between Changmen and Tiger Hill. Exact individual bridge name left unresolved.
new_candidates.guard: Replaced Three Bridges, One Canal title; no claim that three bridges appear in this crop or this one has a proven historical name. Does not reuse bridge inside existing #12 box.
new_candidates.zoom: 380 x 440 detail. At native scale the arched opening is clear; retain the boat and banks in context. 1255 native px from existing #12 center; story covers arch function rather than parallel streets.
